To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
maternal dietary intake during pregnancy shapes the infant gut microbiome at delivery, which persists through the early infant period.
maternal diet during pregnancy and lactations shapes the early infant gut microbiota.
a maternal high-fat dietary intake during pregnancy is associated with a distinct gut microbiome in the infant at birth, which persists through 4–8 weeks of age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the early infant gut microbiota on the development of metabolic diseases.
the effects of a maternal high-fat (HF) diet on the infant gut microbiome and its association with infant growth and development.
how a maternal high-fat dietary intake in early life impacts the neonatal and juvenile gut microbiome, and the subsequent health of the child.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the maternal diet during pregnancy is associated with a distinct neonatal gut microbiota at birth, and that these changes in microbial community structure are sustained through the first month of life.
the early infant gut microbiota varies by maternal diet during gestation.
the neonate gut microbiome is significantly different in infants born to mothers consuming a maternal high fat diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
maternal diet during pregnancy and lactational period has an impact on the neonatal microbiome, which is associated with a higher risk of obesity and diabetes in later life.
maternal high fat diet during pregnancy and early lactation is associated with a distinct early infant gut microbiota that persists through the early postnatal period.
a maternal high-fat (≥40 %) gestational diet is associated with an increased abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, and a decreased abundance of Actinobacteria in the neonatal stool microbiome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
maternal dietary patterns can influence the infant’s microbiome and that the infant microbiome can be influenced by the mother’s diet during pregnancy.
the early infant gut microbiota is not sterile and is influenced by the mother’s diet during pregnancy.
the neonatal gut is not sterile, and the maternal diet is a significant determinant of early life microbiome composition.
